https://nineoclock.ro/nicusor-dan-psd-pn.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Romania’s four governing parties have failed to reach a political and social agreement on the country’s new public sector pay law, President Nicușor Dan announced on Wednesday. The President said the Presidential Administration had been mediating discussions between the Social Democratic Party (PSD), National Liberal Party (PNL), Save Romania Union (USR) and Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR) since May, but the negotiations ultimately failed to produce a consensus. The reform is considered essential for Romania’s entire public sector. According to Nicușor Dan, however, the issue should not have been postponed for years, starting in 2022. The delays have now left the parties under significant time pressure while attempting to address a reform with major social and economic implications. Despite the lack of a final political agreement, the President acknowledged the willingness of the parties and ministerial teams to engage in dialogue and highlighted the intensive work carried out over the past several months. One of the key decisions reached by the four parties was not to submit separate versions of the pay law to Parliament. As part of their political agreement, the parties have jointly assumed the loss of the €770 million associated with this PNRR milestone. More importantly, the parties have committed to adopting the new pay law by the end of 2026 and to respecting the overall wage bill agreed with the European Commission. The available funding, however, will not be sufficient to meet all demands from trade unions. The discussions held in recent months have clarified many of the technical aspects of the legislation, which the President said is now almost technically complete. The remaining challenge is therefore largely political: deciding how the available wage budget will be distributed among the different professional categories within Romania’s public sector. This decision will ultimately determine the level of income for each category of public employees. The negotiations over public sector pay are therefore entering a crucial phase. While the technical work on the legislation is close to completion, the political parties still need to agree on how the available funds will be allocated. President Nicușor Dan’s statement Press statement by the President of Romania, Nicușor Dan August 26, 2026 “Starting in May, the Presidential Administration mediated discussions between PSD, PNL, USR and UDMR on the public sector pay law. Unfortunately, despite intense negotiations over the past several months, the four parties have not reached a political and social consensus on the law. This essential reform for the entire public sector should not have been postponed year after year, starting in 2022. We have thus reached a situation in which such a complicated issue, with major social and economic implications, is being debated under enormous time pressure. I must nevertheless acknowledge the willingness of the parties and ministerial teams to engage in dialogue, as well as the intensive work they have carried out. It should also be noted that the parties have honored their commitment not to separately submit a draft law to Parliament, jointly assuming, in accordance with the political agreement, the loss of the €770 million associated with this PNRR milestone. Most importantly, the parties have committed to adopting the law by the end of this year and to respecting, through the future pay law, the wage bill agreed with the European Commission. This wage bill will not be able to meet all trade union demands. The work carried out over these months and the discussions with trade unions have clarified many technical aspects, with the law now almost technically finalized. The political decision of the parties will determine how the wage bill will be distributed among the various professional categories and, consequently, the level of income for each professional category within the public sector.” Source: Presidential Administration of Romania The diplomatic daily newspaper Nine O’Clock does not assume responsibility for the information received and published on the public website. https://www.theguardian.com/global-devel.text: Abdiqadir Salah and his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled. ‘I didn’t know people like this existed,’ she says of the people who raised the money for her son’s surgery. Photograph: Mohamed Gabobe View image in fullscreen Abdiqadir Salah and his mother, Marian Haji Abdi Guled. ‘I didn’t know people like this existed,’ she says of the people who raised the money for her son’s surgery. Photograph: Mohamed Gabobe Global development Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu Supported by About this content Mohamed Gabobe in Mogadishu Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 5 Oct 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived. Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children. Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back. Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation . For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it. After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery. Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries. “I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said. “The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.” On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu. “Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.” Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition. When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.” View image in fullscreen Doctors took out two pieces of shrapnel from Abdiqadir Salah’s back but could not remove a third. Photograph: Mohamed Gabobe The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack. In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America , a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town. “We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].” With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed. She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said. “I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.” Explore more on these topics Global development Somalia Drones (military) US foreign policy Africa Middle East and north Africa Philanthropy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjx2.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Employees of DTEK energy company in Ukraine work to restore power supply following a missile strike in July By Steve Rosenberg BBC Russia editor Published 9 hours ago On Sunday, US President Donald Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure "effective immediately". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky suggested it was "news for me", while Russia has not commented publicly. So who is saying what? Donald Trump says an energy ceasefire has been agreed. Kyiv asks: Has it? It is willing to sign up â if Russia does. Russia is saying: Very little. Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked whether such a ceasefire had been agreed during his daily conference call with journalists. "Contacts are continuing," Peskov replied. "As soon as we have anything to say about this, we will definitely inform you." Peskov may not have had much to say on the matter, but the pro-Kremlin media has. It has dubbed President Trump's announcement of an energy ceasefire "a gift" for Moscow. "Of course we benefit," pro-government news outlet Moskovsky Komsomolets concluded. "It means that all Russia has to do is not destroy Ukraine's last remaining oil refinery. "That has already been attacked several times. It's barely functioning anyway. "But Kyiv won't be allowed to hit the multitude of refineries we have. "In effect it's a one-way deal that benefits us. That's why no one here has officially rejected it." In other words, Moscow believes Trump's announcement ties Ukraine's hands, not Russia's. In recent months, long-range Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities have caused extensive damage, as well as fuel shortages across the country. Should such attacks continue, expect the Russians to claim that Kyiv is harming US economic interests â as well as the Republican Party's chances in the midterm elections in November. Russian officials will argue that the strikes undermine the recent Trump-Putin fuel deal for the US to import Russian diesel . Trump has claimed the agreement will benefit US consumers, although there is widespread scepticism that the volumes involved will do much to lower fuel prices. Image source, SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Vladimir Putin has shown little desire to stop the fighting Still, the Kremlin will be only too happy if Ukrainian drone strikes on oil facilities spark fury in the White House and curtail US support for Kyiv. Moscow would welcome Washington cutting off intelligence sharing to Ukraine and weapons sales to Europe that are destined for Kyiv. It has already delighted to hear Trump declaring: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called for a 60-day Russian ceasefire to allow for presidential elections in Ukraine. Moscow's reaction? "The Kremlin, the president, has said many times before, we don't want a ceasefire, we want a lasting peace, and we're willing to do whatever's possible for that," Peskov said. "Whatever's possible" does not include a 60-day ceasefire, or a 30-day ceasefire, or anything close to that. On Monday, the Kremlin proposed a one-day cessation of hostilities for Ukraine to hold elections. That will not be seen in Ukraine, or in the West, as a serious offer. It comes as no surprise though. Putin has shown little desire to halt the fighting. Recent statements, speeches and signals from Russia's leader suggest that, with winter approaching, the Kremlin is counting on a continued campaign of Russian strikes to significantly increase the pressure on Ukraine. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. The Kremlin has claimed to seek "lasting peace" but right now it is continuing the fighting. On Monday, Zelensky claimed that Russia had hit several energy targets across Ukraine during the night and into the morning. "This window of opportunity should be used to knock Ukraine back to the Stone Age and force it to accept peace on Russia's terms," the pro-government Moskovsky Komsomolets has written. The Kremlin's objective hasn't changed: Ukraine's capitulation. Moscow seems to believe that the diesel deal with Trump and the US president's growing impatience with Zelensky will help Russia secure its goal. https://newsregister.com/article?article.text: Home News & Features All News/Features Business Education Crime & Courts Nonprofits/Service Stopping By Who's In Jail Crime Reports Map Government Calendar News Archive Sports Opinion Opinion Home Commentary Editorials Letters Submit Letter Whatchamacolumn Community Community Hub Community Links Helping Hands Government Calendar Obituaries Milestones Cities McMinnville Amity Dayton Lafayette Newberg/Dundee Yamhill/Carlton West Valley Event Calendars Community Events Live Music Submit Event N-R Press Club Sign-Up Clubhouse Classified Ads Legal Notices Special Sections Visitor Guide Marketplace Business Directory Classifieds Half Crazy Deals Buy Photos Buy Posters E-Edition News Archives Contact Us Staff Lists Advertise Subscribe About us Support NR • October 16, 2026 Tweet Joel Marrant: The devastating reality of an oppressive police state Wikimedia Commons##Nicolae Ceausescu with Kim Il Sung of North Korea in 1978. ##Joel Marrant About the writer : Joel Marrant was born in Venice Beach, California. He and Susan Earley met as undergraduates at the University of California Santa Cruz. They married and moved to Eugene, where he earned an M.A. and Ph.D. in anthropology. He joined the Linfield faculty in 1978 as its first anthropology professor, and continued until his retirement in 2007, with a primary research focus on the folk traditions of Romanian villagers. He lives in McMinnville with his artist companion, Patricia Schmidt, children Anna Barsotti and Nick Marrant, and five grandchildren all within laughing distance. As a young man, I and my wife Susan had the privilege of living in a police state for three and a half years, one of those years with our two toddler children. Much of our time was spent in a small village in the Maramures region of Romania. At the time, Romania was ruled by Putin-like dictator Nicolae Ceausescu, and his ruthless authoritarian regime was firmly entrenched. He had followed to the letter the fascist playbook for gaining and holding power forcibly. I call this a “privilege” because it opened our eyes forever to the real threat of authoritarian regimes and the damage they can do to human bodies, minds and spirits. Yet we had it easy. Our circumstances in those years as “welcomed guests” of the government presented us with get-out-of-jail-free cards. Romanian citizens were not so fortunate. As the case was then, had been before and has been since for millions of people of all nationalities, escape was nearly impossible. The forces and mechanisms driving authoritarianism are the same. Unless one has personally experienced such suppression of the most basic of freedoms, as did many of our own ancestors, the devastating reality is difficult to comprehend. One of the most pernicious remains the weaponization of fear by those who muscle their way into power, driving our most positive human motivations down and away from our humanity. When coupled with inequities of power, fear runs like a thick vein of toxins through layers of cultural growth and social change. Those who have experienced brutal authoritarian police states like Ceausescu’s Romania, as well as those who sought refuge from them, the poison is obvious. If we choose to look seriously at our own nation’s history to the present, we see where fear has been instilled by brute force, having horrific impact on vulnerable populations — fear of martial brutality; fear of separation from family; fear of relocation and removal to detention centers. Yet there is another kind of fear, even more insidious, that moves sideways, pitting friends, relatives, neighbors and other members of the community against each other. It has the potential to shred irreparably the social fabric of a society, to the benefit of power-hungry leaders who promote subversive process. We saw the crucible of this fear at work in Romanian kitchens 50 years ago. People would gather with the windows closed, curtains drawn, doors shut tightly, radio on and voices low. In these rooms, good people just trying to live decent lives were not only hiding their conversations from government agents. They were fearful their tenement mates, neighbors and friends, coerced or rewarded in doing so, would report to security police jokes overheard about Ceausescu’s evil wife, complaints aired about breadlines or other equally “treasonous” comments. Trust, the shared principle underlying the truth-seeking that bonds individuals within communities, had been sabotaged. And 37 years after Ceausescu’s execution, the consequences still ripple through Romanian society. In fact, they still roil the waters wherever authoritarian regimes have succeeded in bringing fear into the eyes of two people passing on the street. No one has caught the dark potential of that simple glance more powerfully than the Jewish scholar, writer, Holocaust survivor and Nobel Peace Prize recipient Elie Wiesel, who graced Linfield with a visit in 1994 as an honoree and speaker. The account below is an amalgam of his written words, his talks at the symposium and my conversations with him: In his harrowing accounts of his family’s experience with the Holocaust, Wiesel described the Easter week of 1944, when the Romanian Jews of the Maramures region were dragged from their homes in his native city of Sighet and its surrounding villages. They were herded into boxcars, to be taken to the Auschwitz and Buchenwald concentration camps. As a 12-year-old boy, he was part of a parade of innocents, forcibly marched down the Street of the Snakes to the train station. Along the way, Hungarian and Romanian residents stood by the windows of their apartments. Some stayed back in the shadows while others gazed out boldly at the prisoners. Wiesel recalled gazing back into the eyes of some of the onlookers. He described them as empty, unemotional, vacant. He said he was frequently asked if he considered the observers to be “evil.’ He would answer in this way: “The opposite of love is not hate, it's indifference. The opposite of art is not ugliness, it's indifference. The opposite of faith is not heresy, it's indifference. And the opposite of life is not death, it's indifference.” In these difficult times, I believe his wisdom provides a place where we can all find peace and sanctuary — if we put the wisdom into practice. Joel Marrant was born in Venice Beach, California. He and Susan Earley met as undergraduates at the University of California Santa Cruz. They married and moved to Eugene, where he earned an M.A. and Ph.D. in anthropology. He joined the Linfield faculty in 1978 as its first anthropology professor, and continued until his retirement in 2007, with a primary research focus on the folk traditions of Romanian villagers. He lives in McMinnville with his artist companion, Patricia Schmidt, children Anna Barsotti and Nick Marrant, and five grandchildren all within laughing distance. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text: Friedrich Merz (left) welcoming the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in Berlin in early November. Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP View image in fullscreen Friedrich Merz (left) welcoming the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, in Berlin in early November. Photograph: Ebrahim Noroozi/AP Friedrich Merz Merz accused of ‘blackmail’ by Slovak PM after demand for Ukraine aid in EU budget German chancellor has signalled he will block budget with no aid deal, complaining that burden is ‘carried mostly by only a few member states’ Jennifer Rankin in Brussels Tue 10 Nov 2026 11.44 EST Last modified on Tue 10 Nov 2026 13.12 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Friedrich Merz has signalled he will block the EU’s seven-year budget unless there is a deal on financial aid for Ukraine, triggering accusations of “typical blackmail” from some other European leaders and setting the stage for stormy talks later this month. The German chancellor’s intervention has angered leaders in central Europe who are net beneficiaries of EU funds but do not want to take part in an upcoming funding round to support Ukraine’s war effort. “What the chancellor is doing is typical blackmail, and I will not give in to it,” Slovakia’s Russia-friendly prime minister , Robert Fico, told reporters in Bratislava. He was speaking alongside his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babiš, whose populist government also rejects taking part in a future loan for Ukraine. “I do not know why he is saying it,” Babiš said, referring to Merz’s position. Merz wants EU leaders to discuss Ukraine’s financing needs at a summit in Dublin on Friday. “We must continue to support Ukraine in its fight to defend itself. This is in our shared vital interest,” he wrote in a letter, seen by the Guardian, to the European Council president, António Costa, who will chair the meeting. “And yet, bilateral assistance to Ukraine is distributed unevenly and carried mostly by only a few member states.” View image in fullscreen Slovak Prime minister Robert Fico (R) with prime minister of Czech Republic, Andrej Babis (L) at the 10th joint intergovernmental consultation with Slovak government at the Slovak National Gallery in Bratislava, Slovakia. Photograph: Zuzana Gogová/Anadolu/Getty Images The EU last year agreed to lend Ukraine €90bn , which was intended to cover two-thirds of its military and civilian costs for 2026 and 2027. But since then, Russia’s relentless bombardment has heaped more costs on Kyiv, prompting President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to call for €70bn to fill a budget shortfall . The EU has endorsed Zelenskyy’s figures and pledged to find €45bn, with Ukraine’s other allies, such as the UK and Canada, expected to provide the rest. Merz last year led an effort to use Russia’s €210bn sovereign wealth frozen in the EU, but the plan was scuppered by opposition led by Belgium, which hosts most of the funds at Brussels. The €90bn loan was the fallback plan. Hungary, Slovakia and Czechia, which opted out of that loan, have indicated they will stay out of the next round. Those three member states have now been joined by Bulgaria, following the election of Moscow-friendly prime minister Rumen Radev last April. The issue of Ukraine’s financing is now ricocheting into tortuous negotiations on the EU budget for 2028-34. Germany , the largest net contributor, wants steep cuts in the proposed budget, while opposing generous EU funding for member states that refuse to chip in to Ukraine’s financial needs. In his letter Merz writes that “a collective commitment … without exception” is an “essential pre-requisite” for resolving Ukraine’s funding shortfall and “discussing any further matters, particularly those with financial implications”. He also states that all member states need to contribute to a “sound” financial perspective for Ukraine from 2028 in the context of the EU’s next seven-year budget, known as the multiannual financial framework. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion A German government official said: “Financial support for Ukraine of all EU member states is essential in order to successfully complete the MFF.” Berlin is also seeking to switch the decision-making process on funding Ukraine to a qualified-majority vote, rather than unanimity, in order to prevent one government from blocking EU decisions. The letter reflects growing exasperation from the EU’s northern member states that are Ukraine’s most generous backers over smaller contributions from other EU member states in central and southern Europe. The task of finding an agreement on the budget falls to Costa, a former Portuguese prime minister. He wants a deal by the end of the year, before elections in France, Poland and Italy in 2027 that are likely to complicate the task. A spokesperson for Costa confirmed receipt of the letter without commenting on details. “President Costa will make time for interventions on Ukraine at the informal European Council in Dublin this week,” the spokesperson said, adding that Ukraine finance would be discussed at a special summit dedicated to the EU budget on 26-27 November.
